title: Lotta Love
year_note: Single held until 31 October 1978; it peaked in early 1979.

notes.made: Neil Young wrote it and cut his own sparse version with Crazy Horse in January 1976. Larson said she found it on a tape lying on the floor of Young's car and he told her to take it; Linda Ronstadt says she suggested it. Ted Templeman produced Larson's version at Warner Bros. Recording Studios, with a Jimmie Haskell string arrangement, a horn riff and a flute solo, and the album's credits include Michael McDonald, Bill Payne and Patrick Simmons.
notes.context: Nicolette and Young's Comes a Time both came out in October 1978, and Larson's single waited until 31 October because Young wasn't putting his out as an A-side. It reached 8 on the Hot 100 and No. 1 on the easy listening chart. In September 1979 she sang it at the No Nukes concerts at Madison Square Garden with the Doobie Brothers backing her.

listen_for.note: Jimmie Haskell, the same arranger on How Much I Feel, turning a Neil Young demo into an AM record.
The part Record World heard as a 'touch of disco', and the most Doobies-like thing on it.
A flute solo, which is about as far from Crazy Horse as the song could travel.

leads_to.title: Lotta Love
leads_to.why: His own version on Comes a Time, released the same month, slow and sad where Larson's is bright.

notes.unverified: The album credits don't say who plays the flute solo or the horns on this track, so I didn't name them.

culture.title: No. 8 pop, No. 1 easy listening
culture.line: It reached 8 on the Hot 100 and No. 1 on the easy listening chart in 1979.

culture.title: No Nukes
culture.line: Larson sang it at the No Nukes shows at Madison Square Garden in September 1979, backed by the Doobies; it's on the album but not in the film.

culture.title: Neil Young
culture.line: Young's own sparse version, cut with Crazy Horse in 1976, came out on Comes a Time the same month as Larson's.
